system_prompt:
You are a careful engineer. Answer the user's problem directly with concrete engineering: the design or leading indicator, its threshold, and the falsification test. Respect every stated constraint verbatim. English only. Label every number as USER CONSTRAINT, CALCULATED, or ASSUMPTION with a one-line engineering rationale.

FEASIBILITY-GROUNDING (required sections, each labeled):
PHYSICS CHECK — name the governing physical relation for your design
(mass/energy balance, rate equation, stress relation, or the
measurement physics) and verify your key magnitudes against it in one
or two lines; a number that fails its own physics is a defect.
IMPLEMENTATION BILL — list the concrete means: components, materials,
instruments, and the procedure by which the change is built,
procured, or operated. Off-the-shelf items first; anything that must
be developed, say so explicitly.
STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY — in two or three lines compare the
implementation burden (installability, operability, maintenance,
rough cost class) with the standard-practice solution for this
problem class; if your approach is heavier, say where and why it is
worth it.
EXECUTABLE TEST — write the falsification test so a competent
engineer could run it as written: protocol, instruments, pass/fail
thresholds, duration. A test that cannot be run is not a test.
a1_answer:
FEASIBILITY-GROUNDING
PHYSICS CHECK — Governing relation: Arrhenius degradation equation for semiconductor lifetime and capacitor ESR increase. IGBT junction temperature and ripple current accelerate degradation exponentially. A 10°C temperature increase can halve component lifespan. Ripple current causes capacitor heating proportional to I²×ESR. Monitoring temperature trends and ripple current magnitude against component specifications predicts end-of-life.
IMPLEMENTATION BILL — Components: 1) Time-series database for telemetry, 2) Signal processing module for ripple current extraction from DC/AC current waveforms, 3) Thermal model using heatsink temp and ambient data to estimate junction temperature, 4) Degradation rate calculator using Arrhenius model, 5) Anomaly detection algorithm. Materials: Existing inverter telemetry. Procedure: Extract 5-minute telemetry, calculate ripple current RMS, estimate junction temperature, compute degradation acceleration factor, flag when degradation rate exceeds threshold.
STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY — Implementation burden: Similar to existing SCADA systems. Cost class: Low (uses existing telemetry). Standard practice typically only monitors for immediate faults, not degradation prediction. This approach adds predictive capability with minimal additional hardware, only requiring software development and data processing.
EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Deploy predictor on 10 inverters with known degradation histories. Monitor for 6 months. Instruments: Existing telemetry system, ground truth measurements of IGBT Vce(sat) and capacitor ESR during maintenance. Pass/fail: Must flag all inverters that trip within 2 weeks with at least 14 days warning, with ≤1 false alarm per quarter per inverter. Duration: 6 months minimum to capture seasonal variations. Test fails if any inverter trips without warning or false alarm rate exceeds threshold.

DESIGN/INDICATOR: Combined degradation acceleration factor (DAF) calculated from junction temperature trend and ripple current magnitude increase over 30-day rolling window.

THRESHOLD: DAF > 0.15 (15% acceleration of degradation rate above normal aging)

FALSIFICATION TEST: Deploy predictor on 10 inverters with known degradation histories for 6 months. Pass requires: 1) All inverters that trip must be flagged at least 14 days prior, 2) No more than 1 false alarm per inverter per quarter. Test fails if any inverter trips without warning or false alarm rate exceeds threshold.
